subject: paediatrics
title: Pediatric Seizure Disorders: Febrile, Epileptic Encephalopathies, and Status

steps.tx: Seizures triggered by fever in young children represent the most common convulsive disorder encountered in pediatric emergency medicine. Occurring between six months and five years of age with peak incidence at eighteen months, **pediatric febrile seizures** occur in children without intracranial infection, metabolic disturbance, or preceding afebrile seizures. The convulsion typically occurs early during the rapid rise of temperature.
steps.say: Febrile seizures peak at eighteen months in toddlers without central nervous system infection. They are provoked by rapid temperature spikes during common viral fevers.

vis.alt: Clinical algorithm flowchart illustrating emergency evaluation, red flags, and triage of pediatric febrile convulsions.
vis.caption: Diagnostic assessment and classification algorithm for pediatric febrile seizures. [Credit: StewardMD]

steps.tx: Differentiating simple from complex febrile seizures establishes immediate clinical risk and long-term epilepsy prognosis. An episode is classified as a **simple febrile seizure** when it is generalized tonic-clonic in nature, lasts less than fifteen minutes, occurs only once in twenty-four hours, and resolves with complete return to baseline neurological status, carrying an excellent prognosis with negligible epilepsy risk.
steps.say: Simple febrile seizures are generalized, last under fifteen minutes, and occur once in twenty-four hours. Complex seizures are focal, prolonged, or recur within twenty-four hours.

rows: Focal onset or focal motor features
Transient Todd paresis or focal deficit
Complex alert: urgent lumbar puncture rule-out

steps.tx: A devastating early-life epileptic encephalopathy presents with characteristic motor spasms, profound developmental decline, and chaotic electroencephalography. The classic triad of **infantile spasms in West syndrome** comprises clusters of brief jackknife flexor or extensor contractions upon waking, developmental arrest or regression, and characteristic hypsarrhythmia on electroencephalography, manifesting predominantly between three and eight months of age.
steps.say: West syndrome features infantile spasms in clusters, developmental arrest, and hypsarrhythmia on EEG. It represents a catastrophic epileptic encephalopathy in infants.

left.title: West Syndrome Diagnostic Triad
points: Infantile spasms occurring in repetitive clusters
Clusters typically occur upon awakening or drowsiness
Regression of previously attained milestones
Hypsarrhythmia pattern on interictal EEG

right.title: First-Line Therapeutic Regimens
points: Adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) or oral prednisolone
Vigabatrin is the specific drug of choice for tuberous sclerosis
Rapid treatment initiation essential to preserve cognition
High risk of evolving into Lennox-Gastaut syndrome

steps.tx: Chaotic, high-voltage, disorganized electroencephalographic background activity with multi-focal spikes provides the definitive electrophysiological hallmark of infantile spasms. Termed **hypsarrhythmia on electroencephalogram**, this chaotic pattern lacks physiological background rhythms. Treatment requires immediate hormonal therapy with adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) or oral prednisolone; however, in patients with tuberous sclerosis complex, vigabatrin represents the undisputed first-line agent.
steps.say: Hypsarrhythmia demonstrates chaotic high-voltage slow waves with multifocal spikes. Treat with ACTH or steroids, but use vigabatrin if tuberous sclerosis is present.

steps.tx: Severe childhood epileptic encephalopathy evolving from earlier infantile spasms produces multiple intractable seizure types. Typically emerging between two and seven years, **Lennox-Gastaut syndrome** is defined by a triad of polymorphic seizures including atonic drop attacks, atypical absences, and nocturnal tonic spasms, severe cognitive impairment, and an interictal EEG displaying diffuse slow spike-and-wave complexes below 2.5 Hertz.
steps.say: Lennox-Gastaut syndrome presents with multiple refractory seizure types including drop attacks, intellectual disability, and slow spike-and-wave discharges under 2.5 Hertz.

left.title: Lennox-Gastaut Triad
points: Polymorphic seizures: atonic drop attacks, tonic, atypical absence
Atonic drop attacks cause frequent traumatic facial injuries
Severe intellectual disability and behavioral disturbances
EEG shows slow spike-and-wave complexes (<2.5 Hz)

right.title: Refractory Medical Management
points: Highly resistant to conventional anticonvulsants
Valproate, clobazam, lamotrigine, and rufinamide
Ketogenic diet provides significant seizure reduction
Corpus callosotomy considered for disabling drop attacks

steps.tx: Brief, frequent staring spells provoked by hyperventilation characterize idiopathic generalized epilepsy in school-aged children. Classical **childhood absence epilepsy** presents between four and ten years with sudden five- to fifteen-second behavioral arrests without aura or post-ictal confusion, occurring dozens of times daily. Interictal electroencephalography demonstrates pathognomonic, generalized, symmetrical, synchronous three-Hertz spike-and-wave discharges.
steps.say: Childhood absence epilepsy causes brief staring spells provoked by hyperventilation. The electroencephalogram shows classic three-Hertz spike-and-wave complexes.

vis.alt: Pharmaceutical packaging and dosing guidelines for sodium valproate oral solution in pediatric epilepsy.
vis.caption: Sodium valproate formulations utilized in childhood absence and juvenile myoclonic epilepsies. [Credit: StewardMD]

steps.tx: First-line pharmacotherapy for typical absence seizures provides high rates of complete electroclinical remission. The primary drugs of choice are ethosuximide and **sodium valproate for absence epilepsy**, with ethosuximide preferred in pure absence epilepsy due to superior tolerability, and valproate preferred if concurrent generalized tonic-clonic convulsions exist. Sodium channel blockers like carbamazepine and phenytoin are strictly contraindicated as they precipitate absence status.
steps.say: Ethosuximide and sodium valproate are first-line treatments for absence epilepsy. Carbamazepine and phenytoin must be avoided because they aggravate absence seizures.

rows: Can exacerbate seizures or cause status

steps.tx: Continuous convulsive activity exceeding five minutes constitutes a critical medical emergency threatening permanent neuronal necrosis. Immediate emergency management of **pediatric status epilepticus** begins with securing airway, breathing, and circulation with high-flow oxygen, followed by intravenous lorazepam (0.1 mg/kg) or midazolam. If seizures persist beyond ten minutes, second-line infusions include intravenous levetiracetam (60 mg/kg), fosphenytoin (20 mg PE/kg), or valproate sodium.
steps.say: Status epilepticus is defined by five minutes of continuous seizures. Administer IV lorazepam immediately, followed by levetiracetam or fosphenytoin if seizures continue.

left.title: First-Line Rescue (0 to 10 Minutes)
points: Secure airway, supply high-flow 100% oxygen
Check bedside blood glucose immediately
IV lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg (max 4 mg) over 2 minutes
Or buccal midazolam 0.2 mg/kg / rectal diazepam 0.5 mg/kg

right.title: Second-Line Anticonvulsants (10 to 30 Min)
points: IV levetiracetam 60 mg/kg (max 4500 mg) over 10 min
Or IV fosphenytoin 20 mg PE/kg (max 1500 mg PE)
Or IV sodium valproate 40 mg/kg (max 3000 mg)
Prepare for PICU rapid sequence intubation if refractory
